q: A 78-year-old woman leaks urine when coughing, sneezing, or laughing, without preceding urgency. She toilets independently and has a low postvoid residual. Which type of incontinence best fits?
o: Incontinence from difficulty reaching the toilet
Incontinence with increased abdominal pressure
Incontinence associated with urinary urgency
Incontinence associated with chronic urinary retention
explanation:
**Stress incontinence** causes leakage during increased intra-abdominal pressure. In women, weakened supporting tissues commonly permit hypermobility of the bladder outlet and urethra (p. 703).
"leakage coincident with increases in intra-abdominal pressure caused by coughing, sneezing, laughing, or exercising." (p. 703).

**A. Incontinence from difficulty reaching the toilet.** Wrong, functional incontinence requires a cognitive or mobility barrier to reaching the toilet; independent toileting argues against this mechanism here (p. 704; application).
**B. Incontinence with increased abdominal pressure.** Correct, leakage during coughing, sneezing, and laughing matches the source description of stress incontinence (p. 703).
**C. Incontinence associated with urinary urgency.** Wrong, urgency incontinence involves a sudden strong desire to void before urine loss, which the stem excludes (p. 703).
**D. Incontinence associated with chronic urinary retention.** Wrong, retention-related incontinence is associated with impaired emptying and a high residual, unlike the low residual described (p. 703).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 703, 704.

q: An 82-year-old man with an MI six months ago and chronic heart failure (EF 35%) is considered for aquatic therapy after a hip fracture. He has mild chest discomfort with minimal exertion on land. Which concern about warm-water therapy is supported by Hazzard?
o: Increased weight bearing in water may worsen hip pain
Vasoconstriction on leaving the pool may cause hypertension
Whole-body heating may cause vasodilation and chest pain
Reduced buoyancy in warm water may limit support for walking
explanation:
**Aquatic therapy** combines warmth and buoyancy to support upright activity. Whole-body heating produces vasodilation, and patients with cardiac insufficiency may experience chest pain; leaving the pool also requires care because of postural hypotension (p. 826). "Because total body heating produces significant vasodilation, patients with cardiac insufficiency may experience chest pain." (p. 826).

**A. Increased weight bearing in water may worsen hip pain.** Wrong, the pool provides buoyant support and can permit walking when land movement is limited, rather than imposing the proposed increased loading (p. 826).
**B. Vasoconstriction on leaving the pool may cause hypertension.** Wrong, the source warns of postural hypotension when exiting, not vasoconstriction-related hypertension (p. 826).
**C. Whole-body heating may cause vasodilation and chest pain.** Correct, this is the mechanism and cardiac concern explicitly described for total-body heating (p. 826).
**D. Reduced buoyancy in warm water may limit support for walking.** Wrong, the therapeutic pool is described as providing heat together with buoyant support, not losing that support because it is warm (p. 826).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 826.

q: A patient with Parkinson disease develops hallucinations and confusion while receiving dopaminergic therapy. Which medication strategy is described by Hazzard?
o: Consider medication review and reduction of dopaminergic dosing as tolerated
Consider increasing dopaminergic dosing as the initial response to hallucinations
Consider abrupt levodopa withdrawal to reduce the risk of neurologic complications
Consider avoiding clozapine because it worsens the motor features of Parkinson disease
explanation:
**Dopaminergic treatment** can contribute to hallucinations and confusion. Hazzard recommends medication review and consideration of dose reduction to a tolerable extent; sudden levodopa withdrawal can produce a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome (p. 946). "Consideration should be given to reducing the total dose of dopaminergic medication to whatever degree is tolerable for the patient." (p. 946).

**A. Consider medication review and reduction of dopaminergic dosing as tolerated.** Correct, reviewing all medications and considering tolerable reduction in dopaminergic dosing follows the stated approach (p. 946).
**B. Consider increasing dopaminergic dosing as the initial response to hallucinations.** Wrong, the proposed increase runs against the described consideration of reducing the total dopaminergic dose (p. 946).
**C. Consider abrupt levodopa withdrawal to reduce the risk of neurologic complications.** Wrong, the source warns that sudden withdrawal can cause a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome (p. 946).
**D. Consider avoiding clozapine because it worsens the motor features of Parkinson disease.** Wrong, the source describes clozapine as an antipsychotic that will not worsen motor features, so this stated reason for avoiding it is incorrect (p. 946).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 946.
ref: Hazzard Ch 61 — PARKINSON DISEASE AND RELATED DISORDERS · Harrison Ch 433 — Approach to the Patient with Neurologic Disease

q: An 82-year-old nursing-home resident with severe dementia, dysphagia, and pressure ulcers has lost 15% of her weight in six months despite speech therapy and nutritional supplements. Her family asks about tube feeding during a goals-of-care review. Her medications include donepezil, memantine, mirtazapine for appetite, and megestrol. Which prescribing approach best follows Hazzard's general principles?
o: Continue the existing regimen because the drugs were previously indicated
Stop the cognitive drugs by class while leaving appetite drugs unreviewed
Stop the appetite drugs by class while leaving cognitive drugs unreviewed
Review the full regimen and deprescribe drugs lacking current benefit
explanation:
**Goals of care** should guide prescribing, and changes in goals or health should trigger a comprehensive medication review. Hazzard describes deprescribing through dose reduction or cessation when appropriate; it does not support automatic continuation or a blanket class-based stopping rule for this individual (pp. 313–315). "Review medications on an ongoing basis and when clinical conditions or goals of care change" (p. 314).

**A. Continue the existing regimen because the drugs were previously indicated.** Wrong, past indications do not replace reassessment when clinical conditions and goals change (pp. 313–314).
**B. Stop the cognitive drugs by class while leaving appetite drugs unreviewed.** Wrong, reviewing one class while leaving the remainder unexamined falls short of the comprehensive medication review described (pp. 313–314).
**C. Stop the appetite drugs by class while leaving cognitive drugs unreviewed.** Wrong, selectively stopping the appetite drugs without reviewing the rest also omits the comprehensive, goals-based assessment (pp. 313–314).
**D. Review the full regimen and deprescribe drugs lacking current benefit.** Correct, this evaluates the complete regimen and allows individualized dose reduction or discontinuation rather than assuming benefit or futility (pp. 313–315).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 314, 315.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES· Harrison Ch 50 — Unintentional Weight Loss
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation undergoes AV nodal ablation and pacemaker implantation after medication fails to control her heart rate. What does this procedure accomplish, and what happens to the need for anticoagulation?
o: Ventricular rate control with discontinuation of anticoagulation
Restoration of sinus rhythm with discontinuation of anticoagulation
Ventricular rate control with a continuing need for anticoagulation
Restoration of sinus rhythm with a continuing need for anticoagulation
explanation:
**AV nodal ablation with pacing** controls the ventricular rate; it does not eliminate the atrial fibrillation. Hazzard states that "ablation of the AVN does not eliminate AF or the need for anticoagulation" (p. 1201).

**A. Ventricular rate control with discontinuation of anticoagulation.** Wrong, rate control does not remove the continuing need for anticoagulation after this procedure (p. 1201).
**B. Restoration of sinus rhythm with discontinuation of anticoagulation.** Wrong, the procedure neither eliminates atrial fibrillation nor removes the need for anticoagulation (p. 1201).
**C. Ventricular rate control with a continuing need for anticoagulation.** Correct, ventricular rate control is achieved while atrial fibrillation and the need for anticoagulation remain (p. 1201).
**D. Restoration of sinus rhythm with a continuing need for anticoagulation.** Wrong, the continuing need for anticoagulation is consistent with the source, but this procedure does not restore sinus rhythm by eliminating atrial fibrillation (p. 1201).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1201.
ref: Hazzard Ch 27 — PERIOPERATIVE CARE: EVALUATION AND MANAGEMENT· Harrison Ch 286 — ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction

q: A woman receiving tube feeding after a stroke develops abdominal distension and pain with a gastric residual volume of 320 mL. There is no obstruction. What should be done before attributing this to failure of a prokinetic drug?
o: Change the prokinetic drug on the basis of the treatment duration
Evaluate remediable factors such as medications and feeding formula
Stop feeding for a prolonged period on the basis of the residual volume
Continue the feeding plan and reassess tolerability at the next routine review
explanation:
**Symptomatic gastric retention** prompts assessment of remediable factors. Hazzard recommends this evaluation when residual volume exceeds 250 mL and distinguishes it from holding feeds when residual volume exceeds 500 mL (p. 431). "An evaluation for remediable factors (eg, medications, high fat-content formulas) should be conducted if GRV exceeds 250 mL" (p. 431).

**A. Change the prokinetic drug on the basis of the treatment duration.** Wrong, changing drugs according to duration bypasses evaluation of medication effects and formula-related factors specified for this residual volume (p. 431).
**B. Evaluate remediable factors such as medications and feeding formula.** Correct, the measured residual and symptoms warrant the source's evaluation for remediable factors before concluding that the prokinetic has failed (p. 431).
**C. Stop feeding for a prolonged period on the basis of the residual volume.** Wrong, the residual is above the evaluation threshold but below the stated threshold for holding feeds; it does not by itself establish a need for prolonged cessation (p. 431).
**D. Continue the feeding plan and reassess tolerability at the next routine review.** Wrong, pain and distension are reasons for assessment rather than deferring investigation while continuing unchanged (p. 431).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 431.
ref: Hazzard Ch 30 — NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION · Harrison Ch 50 — Unintentional Weight Loss
chapterTitle: NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION

q: A 79-year-old woman with heart failure (ejection fraction 35%), mild cognitive impairment, and creatinine clearance 42 mL/min attends a palliative care clinic. She lives alone, recently began using a walker, and missed medication twice this week. She wants to maintain independence and avoid nursing home admission. Which advance care planning question identifies a surrogate decision maker?
o: Would you want cardiopulmonary resuscitation if your heart stopped?
Whom do you trust to decide if you lose capacity?
Would you want artificial nutrition if you could not eat?
Would you want mechanical ventilation if you could not breathe?
explanation:
**Surrogate identification** establishes who can help apply the patient's goals if decisional capacity is lost. Hazzard asks: "Is there someone you trust to be involved in making medical decisions on your behalf, if you are not able to do so?" (p. 114). Treatment preferences and selection of a decision maker are distinct parts of planning (p. 114).

**A. Would you want cardiopulmonary resuscitation if your heart stopped?.** Wrong, this asks about a treatment preference, rather than identifying a trusted decision maker (p. 114).
**B. Whom do you trust to decide if you lose capacity?.** Correct, this identifies the trusted person who would make decisions if the patient lost decisional capacity (p. 114).
**C. Would you want artificial nutrition if you could not eat?.** Wrong, this records a preference for a treatment; it does not identify who would apply the patient's goals (p. 114).
**D. Would you want mechanical ventilation if you could not breathe?.** Wrong, this asks about a treatment rather than the person trusted to make decisions (p. 114).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 114.
ref: Hazzard Ch 7 — DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST
chapterTitle: DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST

q: An older woman has persistent neuropathic facial pain and cannot tolerate anticonvulsant treatment because of sedation. After appropriate assessment, a nerve block is considered. Which role does Hazzard describe for the block?
o: To identify a vascular lesion and assess trigeminal nerve compression
To identify an intracranial mass and guide its anatomical classification
To localize the pain source and reduce pain intensity or frequency
To localize the pain source and predict a permanent treatment response
explanation:
**Nerve blocks** can serve diagnostic and therapeutic purposes: localization of the pain source and reduction of pain intensity or frequency (p. 1067). Their duration of benefit varies: "the duration of relief with a nerve block can be variable"; MRI with a trigeminal protocol is the investigation described for a mass lesion or vascular compression (p. 1067).

**A. To identify a vascular lesion and assess trigeminal nerve compression.** Wrong, MRI with a trigeminal protocol, rather than a nerve block, is recommended to evaluate vascular compression (p. 1067).
**B. To identify an intracranial mass and guide its anatomical classification.** Wrong, MRI is the investigation recommended to rule out a mass lesion; the block’s diagnostic role is pain localization (p. 1067).
**C. To localize the pain source and reduce pain intensity or frequency.** Correct, these are the diagnostic and therapeutic functions expressly described (p. 1067).
**D. To localize the pain source and predict a permanent treatment response.** Wrong, localization is supported, but the variable duration of relief does not establish a permanent response (p. 1067).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1067.
ref: Hazzard Ch 68 — PAIN MANAGEMENT · Harrison Ch 375 — The Vasculitis Syndromes

q: בן 75, עם דומיננטיות ימנית התקבל עם אוטם ב- MCA, לפי המאמר Stroke Rehabilitation Clinician Handbook 2020 מאת Teasell et al, מהי הפגיעה הצפויה?
o: בפגיעה ב- RT MCA, בחלק המטופלים יתכן Neglect
בפגיעה ב- RT MCA, צפויה אפאזיה גלובלית
בפגיעה ב- LT MCA, צפויה פגיעה בראיה
בפגיעה ב- LT MCA, צפויה פגיעה בולטת יותר ברגל בהשוואה ליד
explanation:
**MCA infarction** may affect movement, sensation, language, and visual fields; the affected hemisphere shapes the pattern. Right-hemisphere spatial processing explains the association with left neglect (Teasell et al., chapter 1, pp. 6-9).
"Right hemispheric: Visual perceptual deficits including left neglect" (p. 7).

**A. Some patients with right MCA injury may have neglect.** Correct, left neglect is described after right MCA infarction (pp. 6-9).
**B. Right MCA injury is expected to cause global aphasia.** Wrong, aphasia characterizes injury to the left language-dominant hemisphere in this pattern (pp. 6-9).
**C. Left MCA injury is expected to cause visual impairment.** Wrong, according to the official key. However, MCA infarction can cause visual-field loss, which the broad wording "visual impairment" cannot clinically exclude (pp. 6-9).
**D. Left MCA injury affects the leg more than the arm.** Wrong, leg predominance points toward ACA territory; MCA cortical representation produces greater facial and upper-limb involvement (pp. 6-9).

Note: "Visual impairment" includes visual-field loss described after MCA infarction. It should be distinguished from the spatial neglect in the official answer (pp. 6-9).

Source: Teasell et al. Stroke Rehabilitation Clinician Handbook (2020), chapter 1, pp. 6-9; https://www.ebrsr.com/~ebrsr/sites/default/files/Chapter%201_Clinical%20Consequences_0.pdf.
ref: Teasell et al. Stroke Rehabilitation Clinician Handbook 2020. 1. Clinical Consequences of Stroke. · pp. 6–9
